lawyer:
Mr. Harendra Nath Nondy, Advocate ----- for the defendant-petitioners
Mr. Nurul Amin, with Mrs. Sakila Rowshan, Advocates ----- for the opposite party No. 1
parties:
Janab Ali Mondal and others
Vs.
Md. Anowar Hossain and others
full_judgment:
Mirza Hussain Haider, J:- The defendant petitioners obtained this Rule calling upon the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the impugned judgment and decree dated 11.2.1999, passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court, Jhenidah, in Title Appeal No. 78 of 1996 reversing those dated 23.4.1996 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge) 1st Court, Jhenidah, in Title Suit No. 58 of 1986 should not be set aside and/or pass such other of further order or orders as may be deemed fit and proper.

2. The case of the defendant-petitioners in short, is that on 29.12.1980 the opposite party no. 1 instituted Title Suit No. 1678 of 1980 for declaration of his title in the Court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Jessore, against the present opposite party Nos. 2 to 5 i.e. the heirs of Godai Molla, Thereafter when Jhenidha became a new district the suit was transferred to the Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Jhenidah on 16.3.1986 and renumbered as Title Suit No. 58 of 1986. The plaintiff alleged that the suit property along with other properties originally belonged to one Kunjo Bihari Ghose under the Superior land Lord Raja Bhushan Dev Roy Bahadur. Kunjo Bihair Ghose while possessing the suit land died leaving behind his only son Rashik Lal Chose who inherited the same and subsequently settled 7.08 acre of and orally, with the plaintiff on 10th Ashar, 1350 B.S. and since then the plaintiff has been possessing the same peacefully. The plaintiff also stated in his plaint that he entrusted one Godai Mollah to help him in recording his name in the S.A. record but the plaintiff came to know on 20th Chaitra 1386 B.S. corresponding to 3.4.1980 that instead of recording the plaintiffs name Godai Mollah got his own name recorded in respect of the suit land in the S.A. Record. Thus after coming to know about such wrong recording he instituted the present suit on 29.12.80. Subsequently by amendment dated 22.3.87 the present petitioner No. 1 Jonab Ali Mondal was added as defendant No. 5 and thereafter by order dated 16.6.1987 defendant No. 6 to 12 who are petitioner’s No. 2 to 7 and opposite party No. 7 herein, were added as defendants.

3. The defendant No. 5 i.e. the present petitioner No. 1 appeared and contested the suit by filing written statement denying all material allegations of the plaint contending inter alia that admittedly the suit land originally belonged to Kunja Bihari Ghose under Raja Promotha Bhushan Deb Roy Bahadur. But the said defendant claims that Kunja Bihari Ghose, while possessing the suit property settled the same in favour of Godai Molla by oral settlement. Subsequently Kunja Bihari Ghose surrendered his interest in favour of the superior Land Lord Raja Promotho Bhushan and since then Godai Molla being accepted as a tenant continued to pay rent in the Sheresta of the superior Land Lord. The defendant petitioner claims that one Rajab Ali and some others instituted Title Suit No. 150 of 1953 in the 2nd Court of Munsif, Jhenidah against Codai Mollah and obtained a collusive sole decree which was challenged. by Godai Molla in Title Suit No. 78 of 1955 of the same Court wherein the said sole decree was set aside against which Rajab Ali and others unsuccessfully moved up to the High Court of East Pakistan. The contention of the contesting defendant is that during the Rent Role Verification the suit property was correctly recorded in the name of Godai Mollah who subsequently transferred the entire property to Babar Ali, Khelafot, Ator and Khotejan. Some of these transferees in their turn transferred some of their shares to some other persons including defendant No. 6. The defendant No. 5 further claims that the said purchasers are all possessing the suit land in ejmali for more than 12 years. It is the specific case of the defendant No. 5 that the plaintiff never got possession in the suit land and as such he has no title therein thus the suit is liable to be dismissed. It appears from the record that defendant Nos. 7,8,10 and 12 entered appearance in the suit and by an application dated 21.3.1990 they adopted the written statement filed by defendant No. 5.

4. Upon hearing, the parties and perusing the evidences on record the trial court was pleased to dismiss the suit by its judgment and decree dated 23.4.1996. Holding that the plaintiff as well as the defendants failed to prove their title in the suit land but, however, the learned Judge found both the parties in possession of the suit land.

5. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree, the plaintiff preferred Title Appeal No. 78 of 1996 in the Court of District Judge, Jhenidah. But the defendants did not challenge the finding of the trial court as regards disbelieving Godai Molla's title in the suit land by "Bondabasta" as well as the title of the defendants on the basis of the said unfounded "Bondabasta" and also the finding of the plaintiffs part possession of in the suit land by preferring any appeal nor the defendants filed any cross objection in the appeal filed by the plaintiff. However, the aforesaid appeal of the plaintiff appellant was ultimately heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Jhenidah, who allowed the same on contest and reversed the findings and decision of the trial court and thereby decreed the suit by his judgment and decree dated 11.2.99. Against which the present Rule has been obtained by the contesting defendant petitioners.

6. Mr. Harendra Nath Nondy, the learned advocate appearing for the petitioners, submits that the suit is barred by limitation as P.W.1 i.e. the plaintiff himself admitted that he tried to record his name in the S.A. record according to him in Jessore area S.A. survey started in 1956 and published in 1957 and knowledge of wrong recording must be during that time; thus institution of the suit in 1980, nearly after 23 years of plaintiffs knowledge of wrong recording is hopelessly barred by limitation. Secondly, he submits that P.W. 1st admission that other than 3 Katas of his paternal property he did not purchase or acquire any property supports the suggestion of the defendants that the plaintiff had no right, title and interest in the suit land and hence he did not record his name. Thirdly, he submits that recording of Godai's name being existing for long 30 years, and supported by the dakhilas, the presumption should have been that the defendants have title and possession in the suit land. According to him the rent receipts filed by the defendants are corollary evidences of title and possession and thus the rent receipts of the defendants following the title of Godai Molla being not considered by the courts below the findings and decision arrived at are erroneous and as such liable to be set aside. Relying on the case of Erfam Ali Bs. Joynal Abedin Mia and others reported in 35 DLR (AD) 216 he submits that when on finding of fact not based on evidence or is based on utterly inadequate evidence or inconsistent with the evidence on record, the High Court is justified in interfering with the same when such misreading of evidence is apparent. According to him the finding of the court of appeal below being based on inadequate evidence the same has resulted error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. Mr. Nondy then submits that the Court of Appeal below misread and misconstrued the evidences of P.Ws. (who were produced as witnesses, without issuing summons) and came to an erroneous decision without considering that out of the five witnesses, three of them stated that they do not know the suit and. Thus he submits that the finding and decision based on such evidences which are not legally admissible are liable to be set aside. He submits that Rashik Lal Ghoseson of Kunja Behari Ghose, was produced as P.W. 4, who admitted that his father Kunju Bihari Ghose surrendered possession of the suit land to the superior Land Lord and as such the court of appeal below without considering this aspect of the evidence, came to an erroneous finding that the plaintiff has been able to prove his case, which is erroneous. The next contention of Mr. Nondy is that the courts below did not consider Exhibit 'C', the judgment passed in Second Appeal No. 572 of 1997. Lastly he submits that the learned Judge failed to consider that without asking for consequential relief simple declaration of this nature is not maintainable. Thus according to him the judgment and decree complained of is erroneous and has resulted error in the decision occasioning failure of justice and as such the same are liable to be set aside.

7. On the other hand, Mr. Nurul Amin appearing with Mrs. Sakila Rowshan, learned Advocates for the plaintiff opposite party No. 1 at the outset submits that this revisional application filed by the added defendants is not maintainable because Ainuddin the defendant No. 6 who has been shown as petitioner no. 3, neither contested the suit by filing any written statement nor preferred or contested the appeal but he deposed as D.W. 2 wherein he neither claimed his on title and possession in the suit land nor he proved the title and possession of any other defendant and as such he having no interest in the suit land cannot have any grievance against the judgment and decree and as such cannot be a petitioner in this revisional application, Defendant no. 5 who is the petitioner no. 1 herein has not properly disclosed his title or possession in the suit land nor he proved his title and possession by producing sufficient documentary evidences to substantiate his case and the other defendants having adopted defendant no. 5's case did not take sufficient steps to prove their title and possession as such this revisional application is not maintainable. Moreover, without filing any appeal or cross objection against the findings of the trial court as regards disbelieving the title of Godai Molla as well as the title and exclusive possession of the defendants they are not in any way aggrieved and they have no locus standi to file the revisional application and disturb the finding of the appellate court which is the last court of fact. Mr. Amin then submits that the petitioner now cannot argue that rent receipts are corollary evidences of title and possession before this court because Godai's title as well as the defendants title having not been proved before the court below by producing any convincing and cogent evidence, which they could also do in the appeal and the defendants having not preferred any appeal challenging those findings, the same remained undisturbed by the last court of fact, thus they cannot now argue contrary to the concurrent findings of fact.

8. Mr. Amin secondly submits that the plaintiff having title and possession through Rashik Lal Ghose, the only son of the admitted owner Kunja Behari Ghose since 1350 B.S. and the possession of the plaintiff having been found concurrently by both the courts below the question of seeking consequential relief does not arise at all. In reply to the submission of Mr. Nonday as to non-consideration of Exhibit-'C' Mr. Amin submits that the courts below rightly did not take the same into consideration as neither the plaintiff nor his predecessors were parties in the said decree rather the same was passed against a 3rd party who is not a party in the present suit and as such the said decree is not at all binding upon the present plaintiff. On the point of limitation Mr. Amin submits that the trial court though dismissed the suit but upon discussing the evidences on record, did not find that the suit is barred by limitation and the said finding having not been challenged in the appeal or reversed by the lower appellate court the same cannot be argued before this court Moreover, relying on the case of Abdul Hafiz and another Vs. Lal Meah and others reported in 8 BLD 497 he submits that the plaintiff is not bound to institute a suit for declaration that the entry in the record of rights is wrong rather he can wait and sue when his right is invaded. Thus he submits that on 20 Chaitra 1386 B.S. corresponding to 3.4.1980 A.D. when the plaintiff came to know about the invasion of his title by the defendants claim through the wrong recording he instituted the suit on 29.12.1980 and as such the same is very such within time and not, in any way, barred by limitation. About the next contention of Mr. Nondy that a finding of fact when not based on evidence or based on merely inadequate evidence or inconsistent with the evidence on record the High Court can interfere when misreading of evidence is apparent. Mr. Amin submits that the said principle also does not help Mr. Nondy, in any manner, because relying upon the evidences available on record the courts below came to a definite finding that the defendants failed to prove their title or exclusive possession in the suit property and it cannot be argued now that the evidences were inadequate or inconsistent when the said finding was not challenged in higher court. There were opportunities for the defendants to adduce further evidence if any, if appeal under the law but they having not availed that opportunity at the appropriate stage now they cannot take advantage of the above principle.

9. Mr. Amin next submits that Exhibit-1, the C.S. Khatian bears the name of Kunja Behari Ghose as a Rayoti Tenant which cannot be surrendered simply by oral pronouncement without compliance of the provisions of sections 85, 86 and 87 of the Bengal Tenancy Act. Thus the statement of Rashik Lal P.W.4 as to surrendering the tenancy by his predecessor to the superior Landlord cannot be construed as complete evidence and as such the petitioner cannot take any advantage of the said statement. Mr. Amin submits that the court below very carefully considered all the evidences on record specially Exhibit-'A' series the rent receipts and came to proper finding that the defendants failed to prove their title no matter Goddai Molla's name was in the record for a certain period but without filing any rent receipt or any other document his title is not proved. Lastly, Mr. Amin submits that for argument sake if it is found that the plaintiffs title through his predecessor's settlement in 1350 B.S. is not valid, which is not at all admitted rather found to be proved as valid by the last court of fact, even then possessing the suit property since 1350 B.S. as proved by P.Ws. and found by both of the courts below, the plaintiff has a good and valid title by way of adverse possession and the plaintiff had been enjoying the same and also transferred some portion of it to different persons and now he is possessing the rest of it along with 3 Khathas of his paternal property. In support of his contention he relied on the case of Sadak Ali Vs. Suruj Ali and other reported in 7 DLR 94 and on case of Sheikh Abdul Majid and others Vs. Dhudar Chandra Chose and others reported in 16 DLR 287. Thus according to him the judgment of the court of appeal below having been based on proper consideration and appreciation of all the material evidences available on record and upon proper scrutinizing the same, is a correct judgment and as such there is nothing to interfere with the same.

10. On hearing the learned Advocates for both the parties at length and on perusal of the materials on record it appears that the defendants did not file any appeal or cross objection challenging the findings of the trial court as regards disbelieving the title of Godai Molla as well as the title of the defendants in the suit land and as such the said finding being not reversed by any competent court the same remains as a final finding of fact thus the defendants cannot claim their own title and possession under the revisional jurisdiction, contrary to what has been found by the courts below. In several decisions it is clearly said that only the error of law cannot be a ground for interference under section 115(1) of the Code but it is also the duty of the petitioner to prove that such error has caused error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. Under such circumstances Mr. Nondy the learned Advocate for the defendant petitioners frankly admits that it is difficult to attract section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure to set aside the impugned judgment on the ground that the error, if any found, has occasioned failure of justice to his clients. He rather admits that having not challenged the finding on title and possession of the trial court it is difficult to say that the impugned judgment has resulted error in the decision occasioning failure of justice to his clients. So in the present Rule only point remains to see whether the court below has committed any error in holding that the plaintiff has been able to prove his case by sufficient evidence, not beyond that.

11. It appears from the record that the plaintiff produced five witnesses and some documentary evidences to prove his case and relying upon all the evidences on record and considering the same the courts below disbelieved the title of Godai Molla as the defendants failed to produce or prove the alleged "Bondabasta Nama" and also failed to prove the date of settlement by Kunja Behar' in favour of Godai Molla or any other date of settlement subsequent thereto by the superior Landlord Raja Promatha Nath Roy as alleged, by producing any oral or documentary evidence nor the defendants filed any evidence to prove that Godai or his successors, ever paid rents to the Landlord before transferring the property to the present defendants. Documents they have produced in this respect is Exhibit-`A' series which show that some rents were paid by one Ainuddin a non-contesting defendant having no interest in the suit land to the Government amongst which the earliest receipt is found to be dated 17.7.1981 which is subsequent to the institution of the present suit though shown to have been paid for the years 1379-83 B.S. and the other receipts are of different dates during the pendency of the suit not prior to that. As such there is no evidence on record from which the courts below could arrive at a decision that Godai Molla had a valid title and after his death his heirs inherited the same and transferred it to the defendants. On the contrary the plaintiff's title through Rashik Lal, son of Kunja Behari Ghose, the admitted C.S. recorded tenant of the suit and, has been proved by Rashik Lal himself as P.W.4. On perusing Exhibit 1 and 2 series it appears that after Kunja Behari Ghose his son and successor Rashik Lal himself as P.W.4 became the owner of the suit land and continued to possess the same and settled the same to the plaintiff on receiving rents from him. Exhibit 2 series, the rent receipts of 1350 to 1357 B.S. received by Rashik Lal having been produced before the Court and admitted by Rashik Lal, clearly show that there is no discrepancy in this respect that the suit land has been transferred to the plaintiff who paid rents to Rashik Lal. Relying on the case of Safar Mia and other Vs. Ajufannessa and others reported in 22 DLR 259 it can very well be said that when no less than the settler himself i.e. in this case Rashik Lal, the son of the admitted recorded tenant Kunija Behari, appears and admits the rent receipts then the primary of the same is already made and the burden of proving contrary or otherwise of those receipts thereafter is thus shifted to the persons who challenges the same. In Md. Yasin's case reported in 2 BCR 16 it has also been held that there is no dispute on the proposition that the onus to prove the tenancy lies heavily on the persons who claim the same. In the present case the onus of proving the transfer from the admitted tenant Kunja Behari Ghose through his son Rashik Lal Ghose to the plaintiff lies on the plaintiff and to prove the same the plaintiff produced Rashik Lal himself who proved that on the demise of Kunja Behari, he as his son, transferred the property to the plaintiff in 1350 B.S. on receipt of rents. He proved the rent receipts, Exhibit-2 series in support of his contention which are the documents showing payment of rent for the years 1350, 1352, 1354 and 1357 B.S. respectively. The signatures in those receipts dakhilas having been proved by Rashik Lal himself, those are rightly taken into consideration by the court of appeal below which decree the suit. Though the defendant petitioners tried to draw some contradictions in the genuinely of those rent receipts by cross examining P.W.6 one Sanaullah but surprisingly Rashik Lal the person claiming to have signed the said dakhilas have not been cross examined on the validity of the same. Thus it appears that the plaintiff proved the transfer in his favour by sufficient evidence. It appears that admittedly, nothing has been produced by the defendants before the court to prove Godai's title by way of settlement by Kunja Behari Ghose or the superior Landlord nor any evidence has been led to prove payment of rent from Godai time till filing of the suit in 1980 to prove that Godai Molla or any of the subsequent transferees paid rents in support of their title or possession in the suit land except Exhibit-'A' sense which is subsequent to institution of the suit which has already discussed earlier. However, in no manner the said rent receipts prove that Godai or his successors had title or paid rent in the suit property or that the present set of defendant except Ainuddin, ever paid rents. Thus such rent receipts paid by another person who is subsequent to the institution of the suit cannot be considered as corollary evidence of title and possession of the defendants and as such, the 35 DLR case, in any view of the matter, does not come to any assistance to the defendant petitioners. Thus in the absence of any such evidence on record the courts below rightly found that Godai and or the defendants claim through him do not have any title in the suit land.

12. The question of surrendering or abandoning the settlement to the superior Land-lord by Kunja Behari Ghose, a reaiyat, though stated by P.W. 4 Rashik Lal, if found to be correct even then the same cannot be construed to have been done in accordance with the provisions of law because the provisions of sections 85, 86 and 87 of the Bengal Tenancy Act has not been complied with. Though Rashik Lal stated that his father surrendered possession to the superior Landlord that is nothing but a statement made by a person again 82 years without any link with the entire evidence as such the same cannot be construed as a complete evidence that possession was surrendered to the superior Landlord nor the same is an admission because his whole contention in the evidence is that upon taking joma and receiving rents he settled the suit property and delivered possession to the plaintiff. Whatever might be the statement of P.W.4 unless the provisions of sections 85, 86 and 87 of the B.T. Act are complied with the surrender cannot be proved under the law. The defendants having not taken any step to prove such surrender or abandonment of the Tenancy by Kunja Behari Ghose by adducing any evidence the allegation, of surrendering and or the statement made by Rashik Lal, will not ipso facto prove the defence case.

13. The defendant petitioners took a plea that none of the witnesses were summoned by the court but it appears from the record that other than P.W. 2 this question was not put to any other witnesses thus it cannot be construed that they were produced without being summoned by the court. Moreover, P.W.2 in his cross categorically stated that upon receipt of summons, through the peon of the court, he has come to depose. So the contention of Mr. Nondy that the evidences o the P.Ws are not proper evidence to be considered does not have any leg to stand. However it appears that P.W. 2 has proved plaintiffs possession in the suit land for last 45/46 years and he never saw Godai Molla possessing the same other P.Ws. also corroborated him. Only thing which the defendant petitioners tried to prove as could be gathered from the cross, is that some of the P.Ws. could not describe the suit land but however, when Rashik Lal categorically deposed that he has transferred the suit land to the plaintiff and he has received rents from the plaintiff and the plaintiffs possession being proved by other witnesses there remains no doubt in the mind of the court below to hold that the plaintiff has been able to prove his title and possession in the suit land. On the other hand the evidence led by the defendants, in no way, proves the title of the defendants rather Exhibit 1 and 2 series having clearly proved the title and possession of the plaintiff, and his predecessors, the court of appeal below rightly passed the impugned judgment and as such no error has been committed in passing the same occasioning failure of justice.

14. Mr. Nondy could not point out any misreading of evidence in the judgment of the lower appellate court for which the above principle laid down in 35 DLR could be attracted. The principle laid down in the 35 DLR case is not in revision under section 115 of the Code where the scope is very limited. But however, in the said decision it has also been observed "Misreading of evidence, not miss appreciation can be interfered with and partial misunderstanding of a document not a case for High Court's interference". Thus on this score also the above citation does not come for any assistance of the petitioner. On the contrary relying on the case of Md. Yasin and others Vs. Kamini Kumar Shome and others reported in 2 BCR 216 it can be said that mere payment of rent to the Government on the strength of unfounded entry in the record of rights will not create valid tenancy in favour of the defendants and extinguish the title, if any, of the plaintiffs. Thus Exhibit `A' series does not in any way help the defendants to prove their case.

<u>15. It is true that the plaintiff is to prove his title in all the cases. But it is now settled that the plaintiff is not always required to prove his title to the hilt rather if he is able to prove his title better than that of his adversary it is enough. Moreover, adverse possession in law is subsisting right of a party, which the law protects and which can be enforced against a person who does not prove a better title. Thus it appears that the plaintiff, in this case have been able to prove better title against the defendants and having possessing the suit land since 1350 B.S. he is as such, entitled to a decree. The defendants having failed to produce any evidence as to settlement made by Kunja Behari to Godai Molla or after the alleged surrender settlement by superior Landlord to Godai they actually failed to prove Godai's title in the suit land and Rashik Lal, the son of Kunja Behari Ghose having proved the transfer in favour of the plaintiff which is corroborated by other witnesses the court below rightly decreed the suit upon finding plaintiff's title and possession in the suit land.</u>

<u>16. Moreover in the case of Md. Abdul Hamid Vs. Md. Fazlur Rahman reported in 50 DLR 441 their Lordships observed "mere error of law without occasioning failure of justice cannot by itself be a ground for interference by this Court under section 115(1) of the Code of Civil Procedure and in that view of the matter we find nothing to interfere with the same". In the present Rule also the defendant petitioners having failed to prove that the error, if any found, has occasioned failure of justice to them there is nothing to interfere with the impugned judgment under section 115 of the Code.</u>

17. Having consonance with the decisions referred herein above and for the facts and circumstances stated above I am of the view that the learned court of appeal below rightly allowed the appeal and decreed the suits upon setting aside the judgment and decree of the trial court on discussing and considering all the materials on record and as such in doing so the learned judge did not commit any error of law resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice:

18. Considering the facts and circumstances stated above. I do not find any merit in the Rule. Accordingly, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. The judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 2nd Court Jhenidah, in Title Appeal No. 78 of 1996 is affirmed.

Send down the lower court records at once.

End.
